theme: Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 26. It is another prayer of David about integrity. Read it carefully, and watch for the way the confident opening gives way to a request for mercy in the final verses.
settingTheScene: This is the last psalm of the unit, and it fits the theme well. Job swore an oath of integrity in Job 31, and David does something similar here. He asks God to examine him and declares that he has walked faithfully. The question is how a sinful man can say such things. The answer is in the last two verses, where David asks to be redeemed. His integrity is real, but it is not his ground of acceptance. His ground is God’s steadfast love.
observation: “Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering” (v. 1).
“Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind” (v. 2).
“For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness” (v. 3).
He does not sit with the worthless or go in with hypocrites (vv. 4-5).
“I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD” (v. 6).
“O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (v. 8).
“Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men” (v. 9).
“But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me” (v. 11).
“My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD” (v. 12).
interpretation:
This is a psalm that raises a question for many new believers: how can anyone say “I have walked in my integrity”? It sounds like boasting. But there are three things to see.

First, the integrity is about direction, not perfection. David says that he has trusted in the LORD “without wavering.” He is not claiming to have never sinned. He is saying that his life has been oriented toward God, and that he has not given his loyalty to anyone else. The Hebrew word for integrity means wholeness or completeness. It describes a life that is not divided.

Second, the integrity is rooted in God’s love. Look at verse 3: “Your steadfast love is before my eyes.” The reason he walks faithfully is that he has been looking at God’s love. His obedience is a response to grace, not an attempt to earn it.

Third, and most important, the psalm ends with a request for mercy. “Redeem me, and be gracious to me.” David has been describing his faithfulness for ten verses, and then he asks for redemption and grace. These are the words of someone who knows he needs saving. He does not say, “Redeem me because I deserve it.” He says, “Redeem me, and be gracious.” He is trusting in God, not in his own record. The same is true in Job, who is declared righteous by God and yet longs for a Redeemer.

The picture at the end is of firm ground. “My foot stands on level ground.” In a psalm full of danger and temptation, the final image is of a safe place to stand, and a congregation gathered to praise.

This is what the unit has been moving toward. In the face of suffering and injustice, the faithful person says: I will walk in my integrity, and I will trust in God’s grace.
connection: Paul says that his own righteousness is “a righteousness not my own, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9). In Psalm 130:3-4 the psalmist says, “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness.” Hebrews 10:22 invites us to draw near “with a true heart in full assurance of faith.”
application:
Pray this psalm as a final prayer for the unit. Ask God to test your heart and mind. Then, like David, say, “Redeem me, and be gracious to me.”

Think about where you have been divided. What would it mean for your life to be more whole this week?

Plan to be in the “great assembly” on Sunday, and sing with the congregation.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to test your heart and mind.
Admit that you cannot walk in integrity on your own, and ask for his help.
Bless him for setting your foot on level ground.
